summary: Wilde's friendship with Frank Harris, from the first thanks for the clothes he came out of prison in, through the repairs of 1897, to what the friendship had become by 1898.
certainty_reasoning: The record documents a friendship or acquaintance with no evidence of attraction or romance; classified platonic, upgradable if contrary evidence comes to light.

sources.quote:
My dear Frank, Just a line to thank you for your great kindness to me, for the lovely clothes, and for the generous cheque.

You have been a real good friend to me, and I shall never forget your kindness: to remember such a debt as mine to you - a debt of kind fellowship - is a pleasure.

About our tour, later on let us think about it. My friends have been so kind to me here that I am feeling happy already. Ever yours…If you write to me please do so under cover to R. B. Ross, who is here with me.
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, [circa 20 May 1897], Hôtel Sandwich, Dieppe (MS Yale) - quoted whole, written within a day or two of coming out of prison and printed on the same page as the letter to Ada Leverson. The postscript is the same discretion machinery: letters to Wilde had to be addressed to somebody else.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The first thanks, and the clothes he came out of prison in.

manuscript.repository: Yale University Library, New Haven, Connecticut

sources.quote:
My dear Frank, I know you do not like writing letters, but still I think you might have written me a line in answer, or acknowledgement of my letter to you from Dieppe. I have been thinking of a story to be called 'The Silence of Frank Harris'. I have, however, heard during the last few days that you do not speak of me in the friendly manner I would like. This distresses me very much.

I am told that you are hurt with me because my letter of thanks to you was not sufficiently elaborated in expression. This I can hardly credit. It seems so unworthy of a big strong nature like yours, that knows the realities of life. I told you I was grateful to you for your kindness to me. Words, _now_, to me signify _things_, actualities, real emotions, realised thoughts. I learnt in prison to be grateful. I used to think gratitude a burden. Now I know that it is something that makes life lighter as well as lovelier for one. I am grateful for a thousand things, from my good friends down to the sun and the sea. But I cannot say more than that I am grateful. I cannot make phrases about it. For __me__ to use such a word shows an enormous development in my nature. Two years ago I did not know the feeling the word denotes.…But I must say again that I no longer make _*roulades*_ of phrases about the deep things I feel. When I write directly to you I speak directly. Violin-variations don't interest me. I am grateful to you. If that does not content you, then you do not understand, what you of all men should understand, how sincerity of feeling expresses itself.
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, 13 June 1897, Hôtel de la Plage, Berneval-sur-Mer (MS Texas), three weeks out of prison. Harris had been offended that Wilde's thanks for money and clothes were not elaborate enough. Wilde's answer is a defence of plain speech as the form sincerity actually takes, and it doubles as a statement about his own post-prison prose. The elision drops a paragraph about the driving-tour he declined. The letter continues past the printed page.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: The friendship being repaired in the open, and Wilde defining what gratitude and directness now meant to him.

facsimile.caption: fifteen sides written at Berneval three weeks out of prison, the sheets numbered by Wilde 1 to 5; the postscript about Lawley follows the signature on the last of them

sources.original_provenance: HRC MSS_WildeO_2_6_067-081. 'now' and 'things' underlined once each for stress; the French 'roulades' underlined too, carrying the mark a hand uses where type would be italic, so it is marked as both. 'me' in 'For me to use such a word' is underlined TWICE - the degree the Complete Letters discard by their own account. The underline beneath the interlineated 'lighter as well as' is an insertion mark, not emphasis, and is not reproduced.

sources.quote:
My dear Frank, I cannot express to you how deeply touched I am by your letter — it is *une vraie poignée de main*. I simply long to see you, and to come again in contact with your strong, sane, wonderful personality.…When you return from Monte Carlo please let me know. I long to dine with you.

As regards a comedy, my dear Frank, I have lost the mainspring of life and art — *la joie de vivre* — it is dreadful. I have pleasures, and passions — but the joy of life is gone. I am going under — the morgue yawns for me — I go and look at my zinc-bed there. After all, I had a wonderful life, which is, I fear, over. But I must dine once with you first. Ever yours

O. W.
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, [end February 1898], Hôtel de Nice (MS Texas), quoted across the page break. The elision drops two paragraphs on the reviewing of The Ballad. Harris was pressing him to write a comedy; the refusal turns into the plainest statement of despair in the late letters, and then swerves back to dinner. 'une vraie poignée de main' is a real handshake.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde
sources.supports: What Wilde told a friend he had left, and that seeing him was still worth staying for.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF pp. 1070-1071. The quotation restores Wilde's dashes where the printed text has a colon or a comma; see `original_provenance`.

facsimile.caption: six sides on Hotel de Nice paper with its engraved pen vignette, a fresh sheet begun at the fifth; the quoted close runs to the signature on the sixth. The seventh image is not the letter but Frank Harris's own printed leaf of it, filed with the manuscript - useful for reading a hand this hard, and headed by Harris dating it 'the winter of 1897', where the Complete Letters give end February 1898

sources.original_provenance: Read at HRC MSS_WildeO_2_6_060 to _065, six sides in Wilde's hand on Hotel de Nice paper; _066 is Frank Harris's own printed leaf of the same letter, filed with it. EMPHASIS: Wilde underlines 'first' and 'signed', both on _061 and both inside the passage this quotation elides. The two French phrases carry NO underline — the strokes near them sit at mid-height, level with the tops of the lowercase letters, and are dashes; compare the rule under 'first', which is tight beneath the baseline. Their italics are the editors' foreign-word convention, so they are marked *thus* and not _*thus*_. PUNCTUATION: six dashes are restored, each written between two words with the sentence continuing on the same line, so each is his punctuation and not an artefact of the line ending — 'your letter — it is' (_060), 'life and art —' and '— it is dreadful' (_064), 'and passions — but', 'going under — the' and 'me — I go and look' (_065). The volume's note on the text says his dashes were replaced throughout with 'normal punctuation as the sense seems to demand', which is where the printed colon after 'letter' and 'under' comes from. NOT PRESERVED: the detached strokes at the right margin, after 'de main.' on _060 and after 'there.' and 'over.' on _065, which fall at the line ending with nothing following them and are artefacts of it. The sentence-ending dash after 'dreadful' on _064 is likewise at a line ending and is rendered as the full stop the sense requires.

sources.quote:
My dear Frank, I do not know if you are still in Paris or not: if you are would you mind letting me have now my monthly allowance for October. I have no clothes but those you so generously supplied me with last May year, and excellent as they are the strain of seventeen months has severely told on them, and I want to buy some more. If you can do this it would be very good of you.

Perhaps before you leave we may see each other, and discuss our Shakespeare - your Shakespeare I should say. Ever yours

OSCAR
sources.context: Wilde to Frank Harris, [end September 1898], Hôtel d'Alsace (MS Hyde) - quoted whole. Seventeen months after Dieppe, and the clothes are the same clothes. Kept entire because the shape of the exile is in it: an allowance asked for by the month, and a joke about authorship in the last line.
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

sources.context: The friendship's early years are believed to have been spent in London from the 1890s, but no source in this record names the city or dates the friendship's start: the four cited letters all postdate Wilde's release (20 May 1897 to end September 1898).
sources.supports: Would settle the London start: the volume prints a letter to Frank Harris headed from London, circa 10 August 1892 (folio 535), and earlier Harris correspondence at folios 469 and 535.
